stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $ABC$?
stimulus: An astronomy student sketches lines between three stars, $A$, $B$, and $C$, to form triangle $ABC$. She then extends side $BC$ past $C$ to a point $D$, so that $B$, $C$, and $D$ lie on a line. In her sketch, the measure of angle $BAC$ is $48^\circ$ and the measure of angle $ACD$ is $115^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: $B$, $C$, and $D$ lie on a line, so angle $ACB$ and angle $ACD$ add to $180^\circ$. That makes angle $ACB = 180^\circ - 115^\circ = 65^\circ$. The angles of triangle $ABC$ add to $180^\circ$, so angle $ABC = 180^\circ - 48^\circ - 65^\circ = 67^\circ$. You can also use the exterior angle shortcut: $115^\circ - 48^\circ = 67^\circ$.

A.why: $65^\circ$ is angle $ACB$, the triangle's interior angle at $C$. You stopped after the straight-line step, before using the triangle sum to reach angle $ABC$.

C.why: $180^\circ - 48^\circ = 132^\circ$ is the combined measure of angles $ABC$ and $ACB$. You still need to subtract angle $ACB$ to get angle $ABC$ alone.

D.why: You added $115^\circ$ and $48^\circ$. The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, so the $48^\circ$ angle has to be subtracted from $115^\circ$, not added to it.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $PRT$?
stimulus: On a site map, an archaeologist draws two parallel wall foundations as line $\ell$ and line $m$. Point $P$ lies on line $\ell$, and point $S$ lies on line $\ell$ to the left of $P$. Points $Q$, $R$, and $T$ lie on line $m$ in that order from left to right. Survey trenches run along segments $PQ$ and $PR$. The measure of angle $SPQ$ is $74^\circ$ and the measure of angle $QPR$ is $38^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Lines $\ell$ and $m$ are parallel, so angle $SPQ$ and angle $PQR$ are alternate interior angles. That makes angle $PQR = 74^\circ$. In triangle $PQR$, angle $PRQ = 180^\circ - 38^\circ - 74^\circ = 68^\circ$. Angle $PRT$ forms a straight line with angle $PRQ$, so angle $PRT = 180^\circ - 68^\circ = 112^\circ$.

A.why: $68^\circ$ is angle $PRQ$, the triangle's interior angle at $R$. The question asks for angle $PRT$, which is on the other side of $PR$ along line $m$, so you still need to subtract $68^\circ$ from $180^\circ$.

B.why: $74^\circ$ is angle $PQR$, the angle you carry across the parallel lines to $Q$. It is at a different vertex from angle $PRT$.

D.why: $180^\circ - 38^\circ = 142^\circ$ is the supplement of the triangle's angle at $P$, not an angle at $R$. You used the wrong vertex.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $EBF$?
stimulus: A printmaker cuts two straight grooves into a linoleum block. One groove runs along segment $AC$ and the other along segment $BD$, and they cross at point $E$. Point $F$ lies on the extension of segment $AB$ beyond $B$. The measure of angle $BAE$ is $52^\circ$ and the measure of angle $CED$ is $71^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Angles $AEB$ and $CED$ are vertical angles, so angle $AEB = 71^\circ$. In triangle $ABE$, angle $ABE = 180^\circ - 52^\circ - 71^\circ = 57^\circ$. Angle $EBF$ forms a straight line with angle $ABE$, so angle $EBF = 180^\circ - 57^\circ = 123^\circ$. This matches the exterior angle shortcut: $52^\circ + 71^\circ = 123^\circ$.

A.why: $57^\circ$ is angle $ABE$, the triangle's interior angle at $B$. Angle $EBF$ is the exterior angle beside it, so you needed one more step: subtract $57^\circ$ from $180^\circ$.

B.why: $71^\circ$ is angle $AEB$, the vertical partner of the given angle. It is an angle at $E$, not at $B$.

D.why: You treated angles $AEB$ and $CED$ as a linear pair and used $180^\circ - 71^\circ = 109^\circ$ in place of $71^\circ$. They are vertical angles, so they are equal.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $DAC$?
stimulus: A linguist draws a vowel chart as trapezoid $ABCD$, with side $AB$ parallel to side $DC$. A diagonal line along segment $AC$ splits the chart into two triangles. The measure of angle $ADC$ is $108^\circ$ and the measure of angle $BAC$ is $30^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: $AB$ is parallel to $DC$, and diagonal $AC$ crosses both, so angle $BAC$ and angle $DCA$ are alternate interior angles. That makes angle $DCA = 30^\circ$. In triangle $ADC$, angle $DAC = 180^\circ - 108^\circ - 30^\circ = 42^\circ$.

A.why: $30^\circ$ is angle $DCA$, which you get by carrying the given angle across the parallel sides. It is the middle step, not the angle at $A$ that the question asks for.

C.why: $180^\circ - 108^\circ = 72^\circ$ is the whole angle $DAB$ at corner $A$. The question asks only for the part on the $D$ side of the diagonal.

D.why: You found $180^\circ - 108^\circ = 72^\circ$ and then added $30^\circ$ when you should have subtracted it. The triangle sum leaves $72^\circ - 30^\circ$ for angle $DAC$.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $FAK$?
stimulus: A sports scientist traces a sprinter's leg on a video frame. Line $j$ passes through the hip, $H$, and line $k$ passes through the ankle, $A$. The two lines are parallel. The thigh runs along segment $HK$ and the shin runs along segment $KA$, where the knee, $K$, lies between the two lines and to the right of both $H$ and $A$. Point $G$ lies on line $j$ to the right of $H$, and point $F$ lies on line $k$ to the left of $A$. The measure of angle $GHK$ is $40^\circ$ and the measure of angle $HKA$ is $75^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Draw a line through $K$ parallel to $j$ and $k$. That line splits angle $HKA$ into two parts. The upper part equals angle $GHK$ (alternate interior angles), so it is $40^\circ$. The lower part is $75^\circ - 40^\circ = 35^\circ$, and it equals the angle between $KA$ and line $k$ on the right of $A$. Angle $FAK$ is on the left of $A$ along the same line, so angle $FAK = 180^\circ - 35^\circ = 145^\circ$.

A.why: $35^\circ$ is the angle between the shin and line $k$ on the right of $A$. Angle $FAK$ opens to the left, so you still need to subtract $35^\circ$ from $180^\circ$.

B.why: You added $40^\circ$ and $75^\circ$. The $40^\circ$ angle is one part of the $75^\circ$ angle at the knee, so you should subtract it to find the other part.

C.why: $180^\circ - 40^\circ = 140^\circ$ is the angle between the thigh and line $j$ on the left of $H$. That is an angle at the hip, not the angle at the ankle that the question asks for.
